papers_seen.author: Lamb
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Context‑Sensitive Engine for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, multi-signal approach for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as the central component of an integrated compression pipeline and combined with complementary primitives (pretraining, architecture-aware design, pruning, quantization, and data strategies), KD routinely yields compact models that preserve much of teacher utility. Its practical success, however, depends on careful choices about what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacity and architecture, how to handle limited or private data, and how to measure and mitigate impacts on robustness and low-frequency behaviors. I argue that KD should be adopted as a configurable, task-aware toolkit rather than a one-size-fits-all recipe, and I provide operational recommendations for practitioners that follow from empirical, theoretical, and data-constrained work in the literature.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Robust and Resource-Efficient Data-Free Knowledge Distillation by Generative Pseudo Replay
papers_seen.abstract: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (KD) allows knowledge transfer from a trained neural network (teacher) to a more compact one (student) in the absence of original training data. Existing works use a validation set to monitor the accuracy of the student over real data and report the highest performance throughout the entire process. However, validation data may not be available at distillation time either, making it infeasible to record the student snapshot that achieved the peak accuracy. Therefore, a practical data-free KD method should be robust and ideally provide monotonically increasing student accuracy during distillation. This is challenging because the student experiences knowledge degradation due to the distribution shift of the synthetic data. A straightforward approach to overcome this issue is to store and rehearse the generated samples periodically, which increases the memory footprint and creates privacy concerns. We propose to model the distribution of the previously observed synthetic samples with a generative network. In particular, we design a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with a training objective that is customized to learn the synthetic data representations optimally. The student is rehearsed by the generative pseudo replay technique, with samples produced by the VAE. Hence knowledge degradation can be prevented without storing any samples. Experiments on image classification benchmarks show that our method optimizes the expected value of the distilled model accuracy while eliminating the large memory overhead incurred by the sample-storing methods.

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of their performance. Work across NLP and broader deep learning has developed multiple KD paradigms—soft-label (logit) matching, intermediate-representation matching, layer-to-layer and many-to-many layer mapping, multi-teacher aggregation, and data-free distillation—and combined KD with other compression methods such as quantization, pruning, and architecture search. Empirical results show that well-designed distillation can yield compact models that approach the accuracy of large pre-trained models while offering substantial savings in parameters, latency, and computational cost. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous teacher and student architectures, coping with limited or unavailable training data, and selecting or weighting multiple teachers per example. The literature suggests principled strategies—attention-based layer fusion, representation-level losses, teacher confidence or dynamic weighting, and synthetic-data generation—that mitigate these issues and enable effective deployment of compressed models in domain-specific and resource-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Pham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical set of techniques to transfer predictive and representational knowledge from large, expensive teacher models to smaller, faster student models. Across computer vision, generative modeling, retrieval, and natural language processing, practitioners use KD to reduce inference cost, enable on-device deployment, and adapt models to new domains or privacy constraints. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate features, attention maps), how teacher and student are aligned (layer mapping, attention-weighted projection, task-aware filters), and whether original training data are available (data-free and zero-shot approaches). Success depends on careful choices of teacher preparation, student capacity and architecture, signal selection, and data or synthetic-sample strategies; when designed appropriately, KD combined with complementary compression (pruning, architecture transforms) yields compact models with strong empirical performance, while important limitations remain (representation mismatch, propagation of teacher biases, low-frequency token coverage).

papers_seen.author: Whitehead
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Insights
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques compress large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, or lower-precision models while retaining much of their performance. Approaches range from matching teacher soft outputs to aligning intermediate representations and using contrastive or projection-based objectives. Practical training choices—such as which layers or features to mimic, how to filter or weight training samples, the role of data augmentation, and whether compact models are pre-trained—strongly affect outcomes. KD has been applied across domains (vision, language, graphs), combined with quantization and low-precision deployment, and adapted for resource-heterogeneous and latency-sensitive settings. Empirical and theoretical work highlights that KD works both by transferring relational/representational knowledge and by providing regularizing soft targets; effective distillation designs balance these mechanisms and tailor the transfer to task and capacity constraints.

papers_seen.author: Briggs
papers_seen.title: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a flexible, multi-signal toolkit for turning large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision and language tasks, KD can preserve much of teacher utility while reducing inference cost, memory use, and enabling on-device or low-latency deployment. Practical success requires careful choices about what signals to transfer (soft outputs, intermediate features, relational structure), how to align teacher and student capacity and architecture, and how to obtain or synthesize appropriate distillation data. KD works best when embedded in a broader compression pipeline that also uses pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and targeted evaluation to detect robustness, fairness, and domain-shift failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Ortiz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Task‑Aware Engine for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood and applied as a configurable, task‑aware core of model compression pipelines rather than as a single recipe. Treated as a modular toolkit—selecting which teacher signals to transfer, how to prepare or synthesize data, and how to align architectures—KD routinely produces compact students that recover much of teacher performance when combined with complementary techniques and explicit evaluation for robustness and rare‑case behaviors. Responsible deployment requires deliberate handling of capacity mismatch, data constraints, and propagated teacher artifacts through targeted adaptations such as multi‑teacher aggregation, data‑free or privacy‑aware protocols, and architecture‑aware student design.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model compression approach to effectively compress BERT by progressive module replacing. Our approach first divides the original BERT into several modules and builds their compact substitutes. Then, we randomly replace the original modules with their substitutes to train the compact modules to mimic the behavior of the original modules. We progressively increase the probability of replacement through the training. In this way, our approach brings a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to the previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, our approach does not introduce any additional loss function. Our approach outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on GLUE benchmark, showing a new perspective of model compression.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted, modular approach for compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD has evolved from softened-logit matching to a multifaceted toolkit that transfers information at output, representation, and relational levels; supports single, ensemble, self- and multi-teacher workflows; and composes with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture design. Practical success depends on deliberate choices about which teacher signals to transfer, how to align heterogeneous architectures and capacities, what data or augmentations to use (including synthesized or data-free inputs), and how to evaluate robustness, fairness, and privacy. When embedded in a task-aware, pipeline-oriented process, KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher utility, but predictable failure modes (capacity mismatch, domain shift, teacher errors, and risks to calibration or fairness) require additional safeguards and complementary techniques.

papers_seen.author: Thomas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: A Conditional, Integrative Argument
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best framed as the central, practical toolkit for compressing deep models for deployment: it reliably transfers predictive behavior and internal structure from teachers to students, and when combined with architecture-aware design and data-aware strategies it yields compact models that preserve much of teacher utility. KD is not a turnkey solution; its success depends on student capacity, choice of distillation signals, data provenance, and complementary compression primitives. A production-ready approach treats KD as the default first-line strategy but integrates it with targeted structural, data, and optimization practices to address known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Montoya
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer information from large, high-performing models to smaller, efficient models to enable deployment under resource, latency, or privacy constraints. The literature has diversified beyond simple teacher→student logit-matching to include feature- and representation-level transfer, online and federated protocols, teacher-free and data-free variants, and architectural co-design. Empirical work across vision, speech, 3D perception, and NLP demonstrates that carefully chosen distillation signals, layer mappings, and training practices (e.g., pretraining, projected feature matching, selective sample weighting) produce compact models that preserve much of teacher performance; remaining challenges include data heterogeneity, privacy, robustness, and automating teacher–student pairing and signal selection.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Multifaceted Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) functions as a flexible, engineering-first mechanism for converting large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Treated as a multifaceted toolbox rather than a single trick, KD enables compact models through combinations of soft-target matching, representation-level supervision, multi-teacher or staged schedules, and data-side strategies. However, KD is not a guaranteed solution by itself: its effectiveness depends on teacher–student capacity alignment, data availability or synthesis, optimization dynamics, and attention to robustness and bias; therefore reliable deployment requires integrating KD into hybrid pipelines that include student pre-training, architecture-aware design, and complementary compression steps such as pruning and quantization.

papers_seen.author: Chambers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Task-Aware Engine for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the central, task-aware engine of practical model compression: it provides flexible signals (soft logits, intermediate features, relations) that, when matched to student capacity and deployment constraints, yield compact models that retain much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a universal cure — it must be combined with complementary methods (pretraining, pruning, quantization, data synthesis) and careful design choices to address capacity mismatch, distributional shift, robustness, and fairness. A principled KD-centered pipeline that selects what to transfer, how to align heterogeneous architectures, and how to manage data and optimization tradeoffs is the most reliable route to deployable compressed models in real-world NLP and multimodal systems.

papers_seen.author: Austin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Default, Conditional Engine for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multi-signal approach for converting large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. When embedded in a deliberate compression pipeline and matched to student capacity, data availability, and deployment constraints, KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs; however, its success is conditional and requires complementary compression primitives, careful teacher–student alignment, and explicit attention to data, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Carney
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses and transfers knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models to improve efficiency while retaining performance. Methods span logits-based soft-label transfer, feature- or layer-wise matching, adversarial and data-free distillation, architecture-aware projection or search, and task-adaptive compression for NLP. Empirical work shows KD is effective across vision, speech, generative models, and language models; recent theory clarifies when and why soft labels help and when mixing hard labels matters. Practical designs—attention-guided layer alignment, projectors or ensembles of projectors, and careful data augmentation or synthetic-data generation—substantially affect student quality. Open challenges include data-privacy constraints, distillation across heterogeneous architectures, preserving teacher errors, and better theoretical/empirical guidance for designing KD pipelines for diverse tasks.

papers_seen.author: Duncan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models into smaller, faster models by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Techniques range from matching output distributions to transferring intermediate representations, feature maps, or distilled data. Applications span model compression for deployment (including transformer compression for NLP), multimodal model adaptation, federated and resource-constrained learning, and improving robustness or fairness. Practical strategies include layer-wise or attention-based projection, progressive module replacement, adversarial and data-free distillation, and task-specific adaptations that account for data heterogeneity and inductive bias.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical, but Insufficient Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile set of methods that enable compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD can transfer final outputs, intermediate representations, attention patterns, or relational structure, and it supports deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD by itself does not guarantee reliable or safe compression: practitioner choices about distillation targets, student capacity and architecture, data availability, and robustness or fairness safeguards determine success. I argue that KD should be treated as the central element of an integrated compression pipeline that systematically combines representation transfer, data strategies, and complementary compression primitives to meet real-world constraints.

papers_seen.author: Webb
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a multifaceted family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention/relational maps), can be applied with or without original training data (using augmentation or synthesized examples), and are routinely combined with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture adaptation. When matched to deployment constraints (data availability, student capacity, architecture, and task), KD frequently yields substantial reductions in latency, memory, and energy with modest accuracy loss. Practical deployment requires addressing teacher–student alignment, optimization dynamics, and potential propagation of teacher errors or biases, and benefits from staged schedules, multi-teacher or ensemble transfers, and pre-training of compact student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Context-Dependent Core for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while often preserving much of the teacher's effectiveness. KD methods range from matching soft outputs to aligning intermediate representations or using adversarial generators when training data are unavailable; they have been successfully applied across vision, generative modeling, recommender systems, and large pretrained language models. However, KD’s success depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, and how to address limited or private data, robustness, and bias—so practitioners must pair KD with task-aware design, data strategies, and complementary compression primitives to get reliable, deployable results.

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Aware Engine for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and practical mechanism for transferring behavior from large teacher models to smaller students, enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is most effective when treated as a configurable core of a broader compression pipeline: choices about what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, how to obtain or synthesize distillation data, and which complementary compression primitives to apply all materially affect outcomes. I argue that KD should be the default backbone of model-compression workflows in deep learning and NLP but must be embedded in design‑sensitive, hybrid pipelines that explicitly address capacity mismatch, data availability, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Mcdonald
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multi-ingredient approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and other modalities. KD operates by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from teacher to student, and is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods, data and augmentation strategies, and careful teacher–student design. While KD can preserve a large fraction of teacher performance and enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, its success depends on handling data availability, architecture and capacity mismatches, teacher artifacts, and distribution shifts. Treating KD as a configurable system—selecting what to transfer, how to align signals, and which auxiliary techniques to apply—yields the best practical trade-offs between compactness and task performance.

papers_seen.author: Chambers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Nuanced Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely adopted approach for producing compact, deployable models from large teachers. KD operates through multiple mechanisms—matching softened outputs, aligning intermediate representations, and transferring relational or attention patterns—and often yields substantial improvements in latency, memory, and deployability relative to naive student training. However, distillation is not a turnkey solution: its effectiveness depends on what is transferred, how teacher and student are aligned, data availability and privacy constraints, and whether complementary compression methods are applied. Viewed as a toolbox rather than a single recipe, KD enables flexible, task-aware compression pipelines that can be adapted to real-world constraints while acknowledging remaining limits around robustness, data-free operation, and principled teacher selection.

papers_seen.author: Haney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Task‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation can be the practical core of model compression: by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teachers to compact students, KD enables deployable models that meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Its effectiveness depends on what signals are transferred, how teacher and student are aligned, and how data and complementary compression methods are used. KD is powerful in practice but bounded: capacity mismatch, data heterogeneity, domain shift, and task‑specific requirements mean KD must be integrated into task‑aware pipelines rather than used as a one‑size‑fits‑all solution.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Is Label Smoothing Truly Incompatible with Knowledge Distillation: An Empirical Study
papers_seen.abstract: This work aims to empirically clarify a recently discovered perspective that label smoothing is incompatible with knowledge distillation. We begin by introducing the motivation behind on how this incompatibility is raised, i.e., label smoothing erases relative information between teacher logits. We provide a novel connection on how label smoothing affects distributions of semantically similar and dissimilar classes. Then we propose a metric to quantitatively measure the degree of erased information in sample's representation. After that, we study its one-sidedness and imperfection of the incompatibility view through massive analyses, visualizations and comprehensive experiments on Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation. Finally, we broadly discuss several circumstances wherein label smoothing will indeed lose its effectiveness. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

papers_seen.author: Leblanc
papers_seen.title: The Practical Centrality of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable tool for reducing model size and inference cost while preserving (or even improving) performance. Beyond straightforward teacher→student logit matching, KD can be applied structurally (transforming architectures without redesign), combined with quantization, used for domain adaptation of large pretrained language models, leveraged in multi-teacher and few-shot settings, and operated without access to original data. KD’s benefits arise both from transferring predictive behavior and from inducing effective regularization; when paired with careful choices (e.g., feature projectors, divergence measures, or pseudo-replay for data-free settings), KD enables deployment of compact, reliable models across vision, speech, language, graph, and generative-model domains.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in NLP and Deep Learning: Necessity, Challenges, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large neural models and transferring desirable properties (accuracy, robustness, or representations) into smaller, deployable students. In NLP and related deep-learning domains, distillation enables the efficient use of pretrained teachers, supports domain adaptation and continual learning, and can be adapted for supervised, self-supervised, and adversarial objectives. However, naive distillation can degrade specific behaviors (e.g., lexical choices or uncertainty calibration) unless the distillation pipeline addresses alignment of inputs and representations, intermediate-layer supervision, the sample-wise effects of soft labels, and robustness transfer. I argue that distillation should be treated as a design problem—choosing which knowledge to transfer, how to align teacher and student representations, and when to expose students to raw or adversarial signals—to yield compact models that preserve both accuracy and desirable inductive properties.

papers_seen.author: Murphy
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, deployment-oriented approach for converting large teacher models into smaller, efficient student models. Across vision, language, and multimodal tasks, KD has expanded from soft-target (logit) matching into a multi-signal toolkit that includes intermediate-representation and attention alignment, relational or contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schedules, and data strategies ranging from original-data augmentation to synthetic or data-free generation. Practical success depends on deliberate design choices—what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, how to obtain or synthesize distillation data, and how to combine KD with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, or architecture adaptation—while managing limits that include capacity mismatch, distribution shift, privacy constraints, and the risk of transferring teacher errors or biases.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: On Representation Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for boosting resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) using more expressive yet cumbersome teacher models. Past work on distillation for GNNs proposed the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which matches local structural relationships defined over edges across the student and teacher's node embeddings. This paper studies whether preserving the global topology of how the teacher embeds graph data can be a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, as real-world graphs often contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We propose Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which uses contrastive learning to implicitly preserve global topology by aligning the student node embeddings to those of the teacher in a shared representation space. Additionally, we introduce an expanded set of benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets where the performance gap between teacher and student GNNs is non-negligible. Experiments across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures show that G-CRD consistently boosts the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a global structure preserving variant of LSP) as well as baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of the representational similarity among teacher and student embedding spaces reveals that G-CRD balances preserving local and global relationships, while structure preserving approaches are best at preserving one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Adapt-and-Distill: Developing Small, Fast and Effective Pretrained Language Models for Domains
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained models have achieved great success in many natural language processing tasks. However, when they are applied in specific domains, these models suffer from domain shift and bring challenges in fine-tuning and online serving for latency and capacity constraints. In this paper, we present a general approach to developing small, fast and effective pre-trained models for specific domains. This is achieved by adapting the off-the-shelf general pre-trained models and performing task-agnostic knowledge distillation in target domains. Specifically, we propose domain-specific vocabulary expansion in the adaptation stage and employ corpus level occurrence probability to choose the size of incremental vocabulary automatically. Then we systematically explore different strategies to compress the large pre-trained models for specific domains. We conduct our experiments in the biomedical and computer science domain. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves better performance over the BERT BASE model in domain-specific tasks while 3.3x smaller and 5.1x faster than BERT BASE. The code and pre-trained models are available at https://aka.ms/adalm.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Default, Task-Aware Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible suite of techniques for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as the core of a compression workflow but adapted to task, architecture, and data constraints, KD routinely yields substantial improvements in latency and memory while preserving much of teacher performance. Its utility spans logits-based supervision, intermediate-representation matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-aware or data-free pipelines. KD is not a turnkey solution: reliable deployment requires complementary methods (pretraining, pruning, quantization, architecture search), careful handling of teacher imperfections and limited or private data, and explicit evaluation for robustness and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Turner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a central, practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. A family of methods—matching teacher soft outputs, aligning intermediate representations, transferring relational structure, and synthesizing or selecting data—enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while retaining much of teacher performance. Success in real systems depends on task-aware design, careful teacher–student pairing, handling limited or private data, and combining KD with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: The Central Role and Practical Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a core set of techniques for converting large, expensive neural models into smaller, faster students suitable for real-world deployment. KD variants transfer soft outputs, intermediate representations, or structural behaviors; they can be combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture modification) and adapted for constrained data, privacy, and deployment regimes. However, distillation’s success depends on principled choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacities, how to obtain or synthesize training data, and how to mitigate teacher-induced errors or biases. Practical deployments therefore require task-aware distillation design, careful teacher selection or adaptation, and evaluation of failure modes such as degraded rare-token behavior or domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Schultz
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for compressing large teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or relational structure. The KD toolkit has diversified from soft-target (logit) matching to include feature- and attention-level objectives, multi- and self-distillation schedules, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows distilled students frequently recover most of a teacher’s utility, but success depends on choices about what signals to transfer, teacher–student capacity relationships, data availability (or strategies for data synthesis/privacy), and optimization/design of the student. Practical deployment treats KD as an engineering system—pairing appropriate distillation signals with student preparation, data strategies, and complementary compression methods to mitigate predictable failure modes such as capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors, and distribution-shift fragility.

papers_seen.author: Branch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Default, Design-Sensitive Core of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the default starting point for compressing large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. KD is best understood as a flexible, multi-signal engineering toolkit whose components (soft targets, intermediate representation matching, relational or attention objectives, online/multi-teacher schedules, and data-aware protocols) must be chosen to match student capacity, available data, and deployment constraints. KD produces strong efficiency–performance tradeoffs when combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful data or teacher preparations, but it is not a panacea: capacity mismatch, data scarcity or mismatch, propagation of teacher errors or biases, and robustness/privacy concerns require hybrid pipelines and targeted mitigation. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as central but design-sensitive, integrating representation-aware objectives, adaptive data strategies, and additional compression or robustness steps to deliver reliable, production-ready compact models.

papers_seen.author: Harvey
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as the Default, Design-Sensitive Core of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) offers a practical route to compress large deep and NLP models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. KD should be the default starting point for compression pipelines because it is flexible, broadly applicable across modalities, and empirically effective when combined with complementary techniques. Its success depends on deliberate, task- and capacity-aware design choices: which teacher signals to transfer, how to align representations, what data or synthetic surrogates to use, and how to validate robustness and fairness under compression. KD is not a panacea — limits such as capacity mismatch, teacher errors, domain shift, and privacy constraints require hybrid pipelines, targeted mitigation, and careful evaluation — but when treated as a central, configurable toolkit it enables strong efficiency–performance tradeoffs and practical deployment of compact models.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multi-level approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD methods transfer information ranging from softened outputs to intermediate representations, attention maps, and relational or contrastive signals; they are commonly integrated with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with data strategies that include real, augmented, synthesized, or data-free approaches. KD routinely achieves strong efficiency–performance trade-offs when teacher–student alignment, distillation targets, and distillation data are chosen to match student capacity and deployment constraints. However, KD’s practical success is conditional: capacity mismatch, imperfect teachers, limited or private data, distribution shift, and transferred biases or robustness gaps remain important limitations that must be addressed through careful pipeline design, task-aware objectives, and targeted evaluation.

papers_seen.author: Matthews
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Task-Aware Toolkit for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Remedies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a flexible, practical framework for producing compact, deployable models in deep learning and NLP. By transferring soft outputs, intermediate representations, relational structure, or synthesized data from larger teachers into smaller students—and by composing these transfers with complementary compression techniques—KD routinely yields substantial reductions in memory and latency while preserving much of teacher performance. Realizing these gains in production requires deliberate design choices about what knowledge to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacity, how to obtain or synthesize distillation data, and how to mitigate risks to robustness, fairness, and privacy. I argue that KD should be treated as the core of a compression pipeline but must be paired with task-aware remedies and complementary methods to be reliable in real-world deployments.

papers_seen.author: Powell
papers_seen.title: The Case for Practical, Adaptive Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible tool for compressing large deep learning models into deployable students. Recent work shows KD can both directly reduce model size and serve as a mechanism to transfer inductive biases, intermediate representations, and task-specific attention. However, real-world constraints — limited or private training data, domain and client heterogeneity, and redundant teacher representations — require KD methods that are data-free, adversarially robust, task-aware, and selective about what teacher knowledge to transfer.

papers_seen.author: Elliott
papers_seen.title: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multifaceted set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models so that compact models retain much of teacher performance. KD encompasses soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate representation and attention matching, multi- and self-distillation, curriculum and data-aware strategies, and combinations with other compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). It has been applied across vision, retrieval, multimodal generation, recommender systems, and NLP tasks, offering deployment benefits under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. At the same time, KD has limitations—capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors or biases, robustness and domain-shift fragility—that require careful teacher/student design, data strategies, and complementary methods. This synthesis summarizes common mechanisms, empirical strengths, limitations, and practical recommendations drawn from recent literature.

papers_seen.author: Brewer
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Design-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a flexible toolbox—combining softened-output supervision, intermediate-representation alignment, teacher design, and complementary compression techniques—KD routinely produces compact models that retain much of teacher performance. However, KD is not automatic: outcomes depend on what is distilled, teacher–student capacity alignment, data availability, and targeted interventions to address robustness, fairness, and privacy. Effective deployment therefore treats KD as the core of a hybrid, task-aware compression pipeline rather than a standalone solution.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Multi-Level Branched Regularization for Federated Learning
papers_seen.abstract: A critical challenge of federated learning is data heterogeneity and imbalance across clients, which leads to inconsistency between local networks and unstable convergence of global models. To alleviate the limitations, we propose a novel architectural regularization technique that constructs multiple auxiliary branches in each local model by grafting local and global subnetworks at several different levels and that learns the representations of the main pathway in the local model congruent to the auxiliary hybrid pathways via online knowledge distillation. The proposed technique is effective to robustify the global model even in the non-iid setting and is applicable to various federated learning frameworks conveniently without incurring extra communication costs. We perform comprehensive empirical studies and demonstrate remarkable performance gains in terms of accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods. The source code is available at our project page.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Concise Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a logits-matching trick into a broad set of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from large neural teachers. Modern KD variants transfer soft predictions, intermediate representations, attention maps, and relational or contrastive structure; they are combined with data-centric practices (augmentation, synthetic and zero-shot data) and complementary compression (pruning, architecture search) to meet real-world latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work demonstrates strong gains in NLP (notably transformer compression) as well as vision, graphs, and federated settings, while theoretical and empirical studies reveal optimization challenges, teacher–student capacity mismatch, and distributional/heterogeneity limitations. Practical pipelines favor pretraining or progressive replacement, representation-level matching, task-adaptive data strategies, and awareness of privacy and robustness trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Harvey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Empirical, Theoretical, and Practical Advances
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central tools to reduce the size and latency of large deep models while retaining much of their performance. Research has produced a diverse set of KD variants — offline teacher-student distillation, multi-teacher and two-stage schemes, online/distillation-in-training, self-distillation, and combinations with pruning — and has demonstrated practical impact across NLP (e.g., translation, question answering, language modeling) and other domains. Work has also begun to explain when and why distillation helps, pointing to effects on data complexity, bias–variance tradeoffs, and the distribution of learned representations across network layers. Implementation-oriented studies emphasize efficient pipelines (to avoid repeated teacher forward passes), dataset-level filtering, and the complementary role of structured pruning for deployment on constrained hardware. Together, these findings show KD is both a pragmatic engineering tool and a growing subject of theoretical understanding, with ongoing research addressing teacher imperfection, optimal training signal mixes, and scalability to very large datasets or distributed settings.

papers_seen.author: Ibarra
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from matching soft teacher outputs into a flexible toolkit for producing compact, efficient models across vision and language. Empirical and methodological work shows KD can transfer final predictions, intermediate representations, relational structure, and inductive biases from large teachers to smaller students, and it is often most effective when combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and when adapted to data constraints (real-data, augmented, or data-free regimes). Practical success depends on choices about distillation targets, teacher-student alignment, and data; remaining challenges include teacher imperfections, distributional mismatch, and preserving robustness and fairness under compression.

papers_seen.author: Lindsey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance

Practical success depends on matching distillation signals to student capacity and architecture, preparing or augmenting data appropriately, and treating distillation as a design-sensitive pipeline rather than a single loss. Across modalities, distillation enables substantial efficiency gains but faces persistent challenges including capacity mismatch, teacher error propagation, robustness under distribution shift, and distillation without access to original training data.

papers_seen.author: Kim

papers_seen.author: Harrington
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a simple training trick into a versatile, task-aware toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often preserves most teacher performance while providing additional benefits such as implicit regularization, domain adaptation, and improved calibration; at the same time, practical limits (student capacity, data quality, and teacher imperfections) require careful signal selection, alignment modules, and deployment-aware protocols. Remaining challenges include principled teacher selection, robust distillation under domain shift or privacy constraints, and scaling KD to heterogeneous, multimodal, or low-resource production settings.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Default, Conditional Engine for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multi-signal toolkit for transferring the behavior and internal structure of large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. As a central component of compression pipelines KD routinely yields strong trade-offs between efficiency and performance when combined with careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which complementary compression primitives and data strategies to apply. However, KD has systematic limits—capacity mismatch, optimization gaps, teacher error propagation, domain shift, and risks to robustness and fairness—that require targeted remedies and rigorous evaluation. This paper argues KD should be treated as the default first-line strategy for compression in production, but only as part of integrated, task- and data-aware pipelines that explicitly mitigate its known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Perry
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior, internal representations, or relational structure from teachers to students. A rich family of KD methods—soft-target/logit matching, feature- and attention-level imitation, multi-teacher and ensemble supervision, data-free and data-augmented distillation, and teacher-student co-design—has been developed to meet deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy) across vision and language tasks. Empirical work shows distilled students can approach teacher performance when distillation objectives, data strategies, and architecture choices are well matched. Remaining challenges include capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher biases or errors, scarcity or absence of real data, and preserving low-frequency behaviors in sequence models. Practical pipelines combine pretraining of compact architectures, multi-objective distillation (outputs + internals), data augmentation or synthesis, and teacher adaptation to produce robust, efficient student models.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesized Evidence and Practical Guidance

A broad family of KD objectives and protocols—soft-target matching, feature and attention mimicry, relational losses, multi-teacher and online schemes—has been developed and empirically validated across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. KD is most effective when treated as a system that aligns teacher and student capacity, chooses what signals to transfer, and composes with complementary primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search, or low-precision numerics). Successful deployment depends on data strategies (real-data distillation, augmentation, or synthetic/data-free methods), student initialization or pretraining, and explicit handling of robustness, fairness, and privacy constraints. Remaining research directions include principled layer mapping for large pre-trained models, reliable distillation without original data, preserving robustness and rare-event behaviors, and theoretical understanding of optimization dynamics under capacity mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Novak

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of their performance. Work across NLP and broader deep learning has developed multiple KD paradigms—soft-label (logit) matching, intermediate-representation matching, layer-to-layer and many-to-many layer mapping, multi-teacher aggregation, and data-free distillation—and combined KD with other compression methods such as quantization, pruning, and architecture search. Empirical results show that well-designed distillation can yield compact models that approach the accuracy of large pre-trained models while offering substantial savings in parameters, latency, and computational cost. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous teacher and student architectures, coping with limited or unavailable training data, and selecting or weighting multiple teachers per example. The literature suggests principled strategies—attention-based layer fusion, representation-level losses, teacher confidence or dynamic weighting, and synthetic-data generation—that mitigate these issues and enable effective deployment of compressed models in domain-specific and resource-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Distilling Object Detectors with Fine-grained Feature Imitation
papers_seen.abstract: State-of-the-art CNN based recognition models are often computationally prohibitive to deploy on low-end devices. A promising high level approach tackling this limitation is knowledge distillation, which let small student model mimic cumbersome teacher model's output to get improved generalization. However, related methods mainly focus on simple task of classification while do not consider complex tasks like object detection. We show applying the vanilla knowledge distillation to detection model gets minor gain. To address the challenge of distilling knowledge in detection model, we propose a fine-grained feature imitation method exploiting the cross-location discrepancy of feature response. Our intuition is that detectors care more about local near object regions. Thus the discrepancy of feature response on the near object anchor locations reveals important information of how teacher model tends to generalize. We design a novel mechanism to estimate those locations and let student model imitate the teacher on them to get enhanced performance. We first validate the idea on a developed lightweight toy detector which carries simplest notion of current state-of-the-art anchor based detection models on challenging KITTI dataset, our method generates up to 15% boost of mAP for the student model compared to the non-imitated counterpart. We then extensively evaluate the method with Faster R-CNN model under various scenarios with common object detection benchmark of Pascal VOC and COCO, imitation alleviates up to 74% performance drop of student model compared to teacher. Codes released at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

papers_seen.author: Combs
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practical approach for converting large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Treated as a configurable toolkit rather than a single recipe, KD excels when combined with architecture-aware student design, complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization), and deliberate data strategies (real-data, augmentation, or synthesis). Its practical value is conditional: student capacity, teacher quality, data availability, and explicit evaluation for robustness, fairness, and domain shift determine when KD will produce reliable, deployable compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Compression and Robustness in Deep Learning and NLP

KD can transfer ensemble behaviour, provide regularization benefits, enable deployment under privacy or communication constraints, and be adapted to domain-specific and generation tasks. Practical KD implementations leverage ensembles, feature-level projectors, data augmentation, self-distillation, or data-free/federated protocols depending on resource and data availability. This paper argues that KD should be treated not only as a compression trick but as a general-purpose training paradigm with distinct theoretical and practical consequences for representation quality, robustness, and deployability.

papers_seen.author: Caldwell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Paradigm for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is the most practical and versatile tool available today for compressing large deep and language models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as the core of a compression pipeline and combined with complementary techniques (representation alignment, data strategies, pruning/quantization, and privacy-preserving mechanisms), KD enables production-ready models that meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints while retaining much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a universal remedy: capacity mismatch, domain shift, optimization instability, and risks of propagating teacher errors demand task-aware design, careful data handling, and hybrid engineering practices to obtain reliable results in realistic deployments.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Learning Compact Metrics for MT
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in machine translation and multilingual text generation have led researchers to adopt trained metrics such as COMET or BLEURT, which treat evaluation as a regression problem and use representations from multilingual pre-trained models such as XLM-RoBERTa or mBERT. Yet studies on related tasks suggest that these models are most efficient when they are large, which is costly and impractical for evaluation. We investigate the trade-off between multilinguality and model capacity with RemBERT, a state-of-the-art multilingual language model, using data from the WMT Metrics Shared Task. We present a series of experiments which show that model size is indeed a bottleneck for cross-lingual transfer, then demonstrate how distillation can help addressing this bottleneck, by leveraging synthetic data generation and transferring knowledge from one teacher to multiple students trained on related languages. Our method yields up to 10.5% improvement over vanilla fine-tuning and reaches 92.6% of RemBERT's performance using only a third of its parameters.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model compression approach to effectively compress BERT by progressive module replacing. Our approach first divides the original BERT into several modules and builds their compact substitutes. Then, we randomly replace the original modules with their substitutes to train the compact modules to mimic the behavior of the original modules. We progressively increase the probability of replacement through the training. In this way, our approach brings a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to the previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, our approach does not introduce any additional loss function. Our approach outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on GLUE benchmark, showing a new perspective of model compression.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical and Versatile Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable compression paradigm that transfers knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller students. When carefully applied, KD enables deployment of performant, efficient models across tasks and modalities, addressing constraints such as inference cost, memory, data availability, and privacy. However, effectiveness depends on what is distilled (outputs vs. internal representations), the availability of training data, and training dynamics; understanding these aspects guides practical decisions that combine KD with quantization, architecture design, and training curricula to produce reliable compressed models.
